tagline.text: A mangrove forest paddle in Palawan's Sabang village, on the way to the Underground River

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (open year-round, early morning recommended)

children.text: The Sabang Mangrove Paddle Boat Tour is a community-run ecotourism activity in Sabang, the jump-off village for the Puerto Princesa Underground River in Palawan. You ride a paddled boat through about 1.2 km of mangrove forest in 30–45 minutes. At about ₱350 per person, it is a popular way to use up the waiting time before the Underground River tour.

The Sabang Mangrove Paddle Boat Tour operates in Sabang, in Barangay Cabayugan, Puerto Princesa. Sabang is the wharf village where boats to the Puerto Princesa Underground River depart, so many travelers squeeze this tour in before or after the Underground River. The overland trip from Puerto Princesa city to Sabang is listed at about
1.5–2 hours

The tour glides through the water channels of the mangrove forest in a human-paddled boat. Each boat carries up to eight people, with a boatman who paddles and a guide who explains the plants and animals of the forest. Sources differ slightly on distance and time, but the course is generally described as about
1.2 km
and taking
30–45 minutes
. Many accounts describe it as a community-based ecotourism project that raises awareness of conservation.

In the mangroves you may see wildlife such as prop roots rising above the water, water monitor lizards crossing the surface, monkeys in the trees and mangrove snakes. But how much you see varies from day to day, and some visitors report seeing hardly any animals.

Waits at the wharf for your turn at the Underground River are often reported to run over two hours, which is why this tour has become a popular way to fill that time. Fees and hours differ between sources and no official notice could be found, so confirm locally. A 2016 blog post says the tour was started by the late environmentalist Jerry Ortega to support local livelihoods and protect the mangroves. Keep in mind that the fee goes toward forest protection and village income, and listen closely to your guide.

blocks.title: Into the Mangrove Forest by Paddle

children.text: With no engine noise and a boatman paddling you along the channel, you can feel the sounds of the forest and the scenery on the water up close. Passengers wear life vests, and you may take yours off only briefly for photos while the boat is stationary. The water is dark green and deep in places, so keep your life vest on at all times. Each boat carries up to eight people, so a large group may need to split up, and one visitor advises sitting at the front of the boat for better photos.

blocks.title: A Guide Who Explains the Forest

children.text: Each boat carries a local guide who explains why mangroves matter to Palawan's ecosystem and which plants and animals live in the forest. One visitor says some guides may not speak fluent English, so keep your questions simple.

Among the roots and branches at the water's edge you may spot water monitor lizards, mangrove snakes and monkeys in the trees. Guides also mention birds such as the Palawan peacock-pheasant and kingfishers, but you are not always able to see them.
A separate bird-watching tour is also offered. Sources differ, quoting ₱350 or ₱450, so budget about
per person and says it must be reserved a day in advance. Confirm times and conditions at the booking desk on site.

After the tour, boatmen sometimes split open submerged mangrove wood to find tamilok (a wood-boring mollusk) and show it to you. It is a Palawan local specialty eaten raw, dressed with vinegar, salt, lime and chili, and on some days none can be found. One visitor compares the taste to a milky, salty oyster, but it is eaten raw, so decide based on how you feel.

blocks.title: A Short Distance from the Beach and the Underground River Wharf

children.text: It is within walking distance of the Sabang wharf; one account says that facing the sea on the main road along the beach, the mangrove is on your right. Sabang Beach and Manlipien Beach, the zipline and Cacaoyan Forest Park are nearby, so it is easy to combine with the Underground River. A 2016 post also mentions a possible jungle trek from the mangrove area to the beach near the Underground River entrance.

items.title: A Day Combined with the Underground River
items.subtitle: Same-day trip from Puerto Princesa

children.text: Leave central Puerto Princesa by van. Hotel pickup tours are listed as departing around this time.
Arrive at Sabang wharf, register for your Underground River turn and get your boat number.
Take the Underground River tour. If the wait is long, you can also find the mangrove booking desk in the meantime.
Walk from the wharf to the mangrove booking desk and board a paddle boat. It takes about
30–45 minutes
Eat lunch at a restaurant in Sabang village and walk the beach.
Return to Puerto Princesa by van.

The order of activities differs between tour operators. Check your Underground River schedule first and fit the mangrove tour around it. Waits at the wharf for your Underground River turn can run over two hours, so the mangrove tour fits well into that waiting time.
Arrive in Sabang the day before and unpack at your lodging. Take note of where the wharf and the mangrove are.
Walk the beach and have dinner.
Board a paddle boat at the mangrove booking desk in the early morning. One visitor says the forest may look misty at that hour and there are fewer visitors.
Head to the wharf in time for your Underground River entry.
Underground River permits are obtained at an office in Puerto Princesa city. Staying in Sabang does not guarantee a permit, so reserve first.
There are flights from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS). Check airline notices for routes and schedules.
From Puerto Princesa airport, take a tricycle or taxi into the city. Check fares locally.
The overland trip from central Puerto Princesa to Sabang takes about
1.5–2 hours
. The Underground River is listed at about
76 km
from the city.
Most travelers use an Underground River tour van. Many packages include hotel pickup, which makes the trip easy.
To go on your own, look into shared vans to Sabang from the van terminal in the city, or rent a car. Check fares and departure times locally.
The Underground River permit must be arranged in advance at the city office, and you pay the fee and receive your boat number at the Sabang wharf on the day.
The mangrove booking desk is said to be within walking distance of the Sabang wharf.
Walk along the dirt road by the beach, past the coconut trees, and you reach the mangrove. Homestays and guesthouses line the road.

The mangrove tour can be done year-round on days with good weather, and it runs during daylight hours. One listing gives the hours as roughly 8 AM to 4:30 PM, but this is not officially confirmed. Sources generally agree that it operates only in daylight.
The quietest time is early morning. One visitor writes that early morning would have offered a misty forest view, while midday is hot and busier.

November–May is the dry season, with less rain and easier travel and boat service. In the rainy season, waves can reach Sabang and halt Underground River boats on some days, so leave room in your plans. Whether the mangrove tour runs may also depend on the weather, so confirm locally.

Sabang has homestays, guesthouses and small resorts along the beach. One visitor mentions staying at a beachfront resort in Sabang; a few well-known places exist, but prices and conditions change often, so check locally. If you plan to start early for the Underground River, staying in Sabang is more convenient.

Meals are taken at restaurants around the wharf and along the beach. The area near Cacaoyan Forest Park is also mentioned as a lunch stop after the Underground River tour. In Palawan, seafood and tamilok, the mangrove mollusk, are known local foods, but tamilok is eaten raw, so skip it if you are not feeling well.

If you stay in Sabang, take a slow walk along the dirt road by the beach. The view of the St. Paul limestone range from the shore is lovely, and the village is quiet after dark, making for a very different night from Puerto Princesa city. It is not clear whether village shops accept cards, so bring plenty of cash.
The earlier you go, the fewer people there are and the nicer the forest atmosphere.
Keep your life vest on throughout, and take it off only briefly for photos while the boat is stationary.
Mosquitoes are common, so use insect repellent and wear light, comfortable clothing with a hat and sunglasses.
Keep your phone and camera in a waterproof bag, and do not lean out of the boat while paddling.
If you want the bird-watching tour, reserve it a day in advance.
Take your trash with you, watch wildlife from a distance and keep your voice down.
Drones are said to be prohibited in the Sabang protected areas, so do not bring one.
In peak season, book Underground River combo packages in advance.
Ask at the booking desk whether the small tree-planting certificate (about ₱5) is available; it supports conservation.
Local guides may not speak fluent English, so ask questions in simple words and gestures.
The water is deep and dark green, so always wear a life vest. There are snakes and monitor lizards, so do not put your hands in the water or touch branches.
Fees and hours differ between sources, so confirm them at the booking desk before you go.
The mangrove tour fits around your Underground River schedule. Work out the timing so you do not miss your Underground River entry slot.
You may or may not see wildlife, so keep your expectations low and enjoy the atmosphere of the forest.
Midday sun is strong and some stretches have little shade, so watch out for heatstroke.
In the rainy season, waves can halt boats at the Sabang wharf, so leave slack in your schedule.
